content: Tuberculous meningitis is a severe form of tuberculosis caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis that affects the central nervous system. The treatment of this condition involves a combination of first-line and second-line anti-tuberculosis medications, depending on the drug susceptibility of the causative organism. First-Line Therapy The first-line drugs used in the treatment of tuberculous meningitis include: Isoniazid Rifampin Rifabutin Pyrazinamide Ethambutol Second-Line Therapy When resistance to first-line drugs is present or when first-line drugs are contraindicated, second-line agents are used. These include: Cycloserine Ethionamide Streptomycin Amikacin Kanamycin Capreomycin p-Aminosalicylic acid Levofloxacin Moxifloxacin Gatifloxacin Tuberculous Meningitis Caused by Drug-Susceptible Mycobacterium tuberculosis Intensive Phase (Adults) The preferred regimen for adults during the intensive phase includes: Isoniazid at 5 mg/kg (maximum dose: 300 mg) daily for 2 months. Rifampin at 10 mg/kg (maximum dose: 600 mg) daily for 2 months. Pyrazinamide at 15–30 mg/kg (maximum dose: 2 g) daily for 2 months. Ethambutol at 15–20 mg/kg (maximum dose: 1 g) daily for 2 months. Continuation Phase (Adults) The continuation phase for adults involves: Isoniazid at 5 mg/kg (maximum dose: 300 mg) daily for 7–10 months. Rifampin at 10 mg/kg (maximum dose: 600 mg) daily for 7–10 months. Intensive Phase (Pediatrics) The preferred regimen for children during the intensive phase includes: Isoniazid at 10–15 mg/kg (maximum dose: 300 mg) daily for 2 months. Rifampin at 10–20 mg/kg (maximum dose: 600 mg) daily for 2 months. Pyrazinamide at 15–30 mg/kg (maximum dose: 2 g) daily for 2 months. Ethambutol at 15–20 mg/kg (maximum dose: 1 g) daily for 2 months. Continuation Phase (Pediatrics) The continuation phase for children involves: Isoniazid at 10–15 mg/kg (maximum dose: 300 mg) daily for 7–10 months. Rifampin at 10–20 mg/kg (maximum dose: 600 mg) daily for 7–10 months. Tuberculous Meningitis Caused by Drug-Resistant Mycobacterium tuberculosis Isoniazid Monoresistance Replace Isoniazid with a fluoroquinolone in the intensive phase regimen. Continue treatment with Rifampin, Pyrazinamide, and the fluoroquinolone for a total duration of 12 months. Rifampin Monoresistance Replace Rifampin with a fluoroquinolone in the intensive phase regimen. Continue treatment with Isoniazid, Pyrazinamide, and the fluoroquinolone for a total duration of 18 months. Multidrug-Resistant Tuberculosis (MDR-TB) MDR-TB is defined as resistance to both Isoniazid and Rifampin. Therapy for MDR-TB should be considered in cases of prior tuberculosis treatment, contact with a patient with MDR-TB, or poor clinical response to first-line therapy within 2 weeks despite confirmed diagnosis and adherence to treatment. Second-line agents, such as aminoglycosides, can penetrate the blood-brain barrier (BBB) only when the meninges are inflamed. Fluoroquinolones can penetrate the central nervous system (CNS) but achieve lower concentrations in cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) compared to serum or brain parenchyma. Consultation with an infectious disease specialist is strongly recommended. Extensively Drug-Resistant Tuberculosis (XDR-TB) XDR-TB is defined as resistance to Isoniazid, Rifampin, fluoroquinolones, and at least one of the injectable second-line drugs (e.g., Capreomycin, Kanamycin, or Amikacin). Consider using Ethionamide or Cycloserine to construct the treatment regimen. Consultation with an infectious disease specialist is essential. References The treatment guidelines and recommendations are based on authoritative sources, including the American Thoracic Society, Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), Infectious Diseases Society of America, and the World Health Organization (WHO). These guidelines are supported by clinical studies and expert consensus on the management of tuberculosis, particularly its central nervous system manifestations.
